hypothesis: A structural key encoding the same future-relevant CLSN1 facts preserves exact-TT search behavior while removing enough string serialization overhead to improve wall-clock performance.
interpretation: The structural key preserved every chosen action, expanded-node count, and cache-hit count produced by the CLSN-string transposition table on the frozen position suite.
The representation change reduced transposition-table wall-clock time to about 79 percent of the CLSN-string implementation at depths 2, 3, and 4.
At depth 2 there were no transposition hits, so even the structural table remained about 9.6 percent slower than baseline because cache management had no work to recover.
At depth 3 the structural exact-TT implementation was effectively break-even with baseline wall-clock time while still reducing expanded nodes by 16.9 percent.
At depth 4 the structural exact-TT implementation reduced expanded nodes by 28.6 percent and was about 5.9 percent faster than baseline wall-clock time.

This supports retaining structural exact transposition caching as a search-engineering building block for deeper searches, while not enabling it blindly at depth 2 where the measured suite shows no benefit.

The result also preserves the architecture boundary: CLSN1 remains the reversible external state notation and benchmark-fixture identity; the structural tuple is an internal performance representation of the same state facts.
